anchors.note: Objection from fallible practical judgment and utility
Reply: utility judgment also requires contestability

nodes.title: On Liberty, Chapter II (excerpt)
nodes.summary: Mill develops a fallibility-based defense of open discussion and answers an objection that practical judgment can justify suppressing harmful error.

nodes.title: Two hypotheses require separate branches
nodes.summary: Mill announces that suppression must be tested under two hypotheses and begins with the possibility that the suppressed opinion is true.
nodes.role_in_parent: Sets the branch structure for the excerpt.

nodes.title: Silencing assumes infallibility
nodes.summary: Suppressors cannot convert their certainty into absolute certainty for everyone; denying a hearing therefore assumes infallibility.
nodes.role_in_parent: States the first branch of the anti-suppression argument.

nodes.title: Objection: fallible agents still must act
nodes.summary: An objector argues that acting on fallible judgment is unavoidable and that governments may sometimes uphold beliefs judged necessary or useful.
nodes.role_in_parent: Challenges the inference from fallibility to a prohibition on suppression.

nodes.title: Reply: utility judgments are equally disputable
nodes.summary: Mill replies that appealing to usefulness only relocates the infallibility problem because usefulness itself is contestable and connected to truth.
nodes.role_in_parent: Answers the objection and restores the case for open discussion.

edges.explanation: The framing paragraph explicitly announces separate branches and the next paragraph begins the first branch.
The objection denies that acknowledged fallibility prevents authorities from acting on conscientious judgments about error or utility.
The reply directly answers the utility-based escape proposed by the objection.
By showing that utility judgments also remain disputable, the reply reinforces the broader claim that suppression cannot escape the infallibility problem.
